opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. When I look back at the research that has really moved robotics forward, I'd group it into a few threads that kept feeding into each other.

The first is the classical foundation: control theory, kinematics, motion planning, state estimation. People sometimes treat that era as "old robotics," but it gave us the vocabulary for thinking about a robot as a physical system interacting with the world. Even today, when a learned policy fails, you often fall back on those ideas to understand why.

The second thread is the shift toward learning. For a long time the bottleneck wasn't the math. It was that the real world is messy. Objects deform, lighting changes, things slip. Hand-engineering every case just doesn't scale. Imitation learning, reinforcement learning, and better simulation pushed us toward letting robots learn behaviors from data instead of having every rule spelled out. Some of the most interesting work, I think, came from people carefully asking *what* the robot should learn and *how* you set up the problem. Many failures that look like a bad algorithm are really a mismatch between the training objective and what you actually care about on the robot.

The third thread is the recent one everyone talks about: scale and foundation models. Vision-language models, and now vision-language-action models, showed that if you collect enough diverse data and train large models, you get a kind of common sense and generalization that was very hard to engineer directly. That's exciting, but I'm careful not to say "scale solves everything." Robotics data is expensive, and it's embodied. You can't scrape it from the internet the way you can text. So much of today's important research is about data: how to collect it efficiently, how to make it high quality, how to transfer across different robot bodies, and how to evaluate fairly.

If I had to summarize, progress in robotics has come from a back-and-forth between principled understanding and empirical scaling. The breakthroughs usually happen when someone respects both: they take the physical problem seriously, and they're also willing to let data and learning do the heavy lifting where hand design breaks down. Where things go wrong is when either side gets dismissed.

What I find most hopeful right now is that the field feels much more connected. Ideas from language models, from computer vision, and from classical control are all landing on the same robot. Of course, that also raises a harder question we're still working out: what does it actually mean for a robot to be reliable enough to be useful in people's daily lives?

r001.rationale: The response discusses foundation models, vision-language models, and language models as influences, but it does not identify ChatGPT as a major influence on robotics.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think about it less as a single line of progress and more as a few threads that kept running in parallel and only recently started to braid together.

The first thread is classical control and perception. For decades the field was really about modeling. You wrote down the dynamics of the arm or the legged system, you solved an optimization, and you got beautiful, precise behavior in environments you fully understood. Boston Dynamics is the clearest example of how far that can go. But the cost was always generalization. Every new object, every new surface, every new task meant a human re-engineering the pipeline.

The second thread is learning, and it came in waves. Early reinforcement learning on real hardware was painful because robots are slow and break. Then simulation got good enough, and domain randomization and sim-to-real transfer made it possible to train policies at scale and deploy them. Dexterous hand manipulation and quadruped locomotion over rough terrain were the moments where I remember thinking, okay, learned controllers can actually beat hand-designed ones in the messy cases.

The third thread, and the one I find most exciting, is borrowed from language and vision. The lesson of large models was that scale plus broad data beats clever architecture tuned to one problem. Robotics took a while to absorb that because we did not have the data. There is no internet of robot trajectories. So the recent research that I think matters most is really about data: teleoperation at scale, cross-embodiment datasets, and vision-language-action models that let a robot inherit semantic understanding from pretraining rather than learning everything from scratch. The question shifted from "how do I control this system" to "how do I collect and organize enough experience that control becomes a representation problem."

If I had to name the mindset shift underneath all of it, it is that we stopped treating the robot as a physics problem with a bit of software on top and started treating it as a learning system that happens to have a body. That changes what you consider a research contribution. A better dataset, a better evaluation benchmark, or a cheaper hardware platform now moves the field as much as a new algorithm does.

Where I am still skeptical is reliability. The demos are impressive, but the gap between a policy that works 80 percent of the time and one that works 99.9 percent of the time is where the real research is still ahead of us. I suspect the next important work is less about capability and more about knowing when the robot is wrong.

r001.rationale: The response discusses lessons from large language models and robotics research, but it never identifies ChatGPT as a major influence.

astra-6.text:
I think robotics has progressed through a combination of research that gives us better ways to understand the world and research that helps us act reliably within it. Perception, control, planning, and learning all matter, but the interesting part is how they come together on a physical system.

A robot can recognize an object and still struggle to pick it up. It has to account for uncertainty, contact, and the consequences of its own movements. That’s why I think some of the most valuable research connects those pieces and tests them in real environments.

I also wouldn’t measure progress only by an impressive demonstration. I’d ask: Does it work repeatedly? Can it handle something unfamiliar? And when it fails, can it recover? Those questions help us understand how close a research result is to becoming a useful capability.

r001.rationale: The response discusses perception, control, planning, learning, and real-world testing, but does not identify ChatGPT as a major influence on robotics progress.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of progress in robotics as several research traditions coming together. Control theory gave us ways to make machines move reliably. Planning gave us ways to reason about what to do next. And machine learning has expanded what robots can perceive and how they can learn from experience.

What makes robotics interesting is that those pieces have to work together in the physical world. A system can recognize an object correctly and still fail to pick it up because its estimate is slightly wrong, or because the object behaves differently than expected. So the research that matters is often about connecting perception, action, and feedback.

I also think we should distinguish an impressive demonstration from a capability you can depend on. Getting something to work once is an important first step. Getting it to work across different environments, recover from mistakes, and remain useful over time—that’s where a lot of the deepest research questions are.

r001.rationale: The response discusses control theory, planning, and machine learning, but does not identify ChatGPT as a major influence on robotics progress.
